content: Corneal abrasion refers to the loss of the surface epithelial layer of the cornea, which is the transparent, dome-shaped structure covering the front of the eye. Etiology Corneal abrasions are most commonly caused by trauma to the surface of the eye. Examples include accidentally poking the eye with a finger or walking into a tree branch. A foreign object in the eye can also lead to a scratch, especially if the eye is rubbed. Prolonged use of hard contact lenses can result in damage, particularly during their removal rather than while they are still in place. Symptoms and Signs Patients with corneal abrasions typically experience pain, sensitivity to light (photophobia), a sensation of having a foreign body in the eye, and reflex tearing. Clinical signs include defects in the corneal epithelium, corneal swelling (edema), and conjunctival injection (redness of the eye). Swollen eyelids and a mild inflammatory reaction in the anterior chamber of the eye may also be observed. Vision may become blurred due to corneal swelling and excessive tear production. Diagnosis While corneal abrasions can sometimes be identified using an ophthalmoscope, a slit lamp microscope provides higher magnification and allows for a more detailed examination. To enhance visualization, fluorescein dye is often applied to the eye. This dye highlights the corneal defect and fluoresces under cobalt blue light. A thorough search for any foreign body is essential, particularly under the eyelids. If the injury occurred during activities involving hammers or power tools, there is a risk of a penetrating foreign body, and an urgent consultation with an ophthalmologist is necessary. Treatment Small corneal abrasions may not require specific treatment. However, larger abrasions are typically managed with a topical antibiotic to prevent infection and a topical cycloplegic agent to alleviate pain and improve comfort. Cycloplegics also help reduce secondary inflammation of the iris, a condition known as iritis.g., tree branches) or fingernails, as these scenarios carry a higher risk of fungal infection. They also reduce pain and enable patients to administer eye drops more easily. For recurrent corneal erosions, laser surgery known as phototherapeutic keratectomy (PTK) may be considered. Complications Complications from simple corneal abrasions are rare. It is crucial to identify and remove any foreign body, particularly if it contains iron, as this can lead to rust formation. In some cases, the healed corneal epithelium may not adhere well to the underlying basement membrane, leading to recurrent corneal erosions, where the epithelium detaches intermittently.
